newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto's party undecided on boycotting parliament.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto's party undecided on boycotting parliament.

text.p: Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto, trying to come to terms with a crushing election defeat, deferred a decision on whether to boycott the national and provincial assemblies after huddling with party colleagues on Wednesday.
Bhutto's triumphant rival, Nawaz Sharif, left for a short pilgrimage to Mecca, Saudi Arabia, to give thanks after the victory of his Pakistan Muslim League (PML) in Monday's polls.
Party sources quoted by the official news agency APP said he would return home on Saturday.
With 203 results declared, the PML had won 134 seats in the 217-seat National Assembly. Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) secured only 19, its lowest tally since 1969.

The result from one constituency is still awaited. Elections in three constituencies were postponed due to deaths of candidates. Results in 10 seats reserved for religious minorities are not expected to be announced for several days.
Bhutto huddled with her party's central executive committee for more than four hours, but no agreement was reached.
"The decision whether to sit in the assembly or not will be taken by the parliamentary party one day before the National Assembly (lower house) session," a PPP spokesman said.

"Nobody minds losing. We feel aggrieved for being cheated," the spokesman, Senator Iqbal Haider, told a news conference in Islamabad. He said the elections were rigged but confirmed that the party would not agitate against the poll.
The National Assembly is to meet on February 15, a day after the Election Commission ratifies final results, to anoint Sharif as prime minister. He may name his cabinet the next day.
Sharif, 47, is starting his second term with unprecedented parliamentary clout -- he and his allies will have the two-thirds majority needed to change the constitution.
But he will need all his skills to rule a turbulent nation riven by sectarian and ethnic tension, weakened by economic troubles and locked in perennial conflict with arch-rival India.
Sharif also faces deep public disenchantment with a political class blamed for earning Pakistan the reputation of being a very corrupt country, though he blames Bhutto for that.
"The winners need to convert victory into national healing and reconciliation," the English-language daily The Muslim said.

The Nation, a Lahore-based newspaper, said the PPP could still play a useful role in opposition. "Clearly though, the manner in which the PPP has been trounced betrays a complete and total vote of no confidence in the party and its leadership."
President Farooq Leghari, once a Bhutto ally, called the election after dismissing her government on November 5, alleging corruption and misrule. Bhutto denies the charges.
Sharif's first government was similarly sacked on corruption charges in 1993 but was briefly reinstated by the Supreme Court before the PPP defeated it in general elections the same year.
He must now decide whether to take on the newly assertive Leghari and use his parliamentary muscle to scrap the president's power to fire an elected government.
Sharif also has to decide whether to go along with a Council for Defence and National Security, created by Leghari last month in what he said was an attempt to ensure continuity.

The council, bringing together top cabinet ministers and generals under Leghari's chairmanship, has only an advisory role. But it has been widely seen as a way to hold the next government to the agenda set by Leghari's caretakers.
Leghari has pledged Pakistan will adhere to the economic programme agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Sharif has promised to keep the IMF commitments. But Sartaj Aziz, tipped as the new finance minister, said on Tuesday that Pakistan was unlikely to meet the tough deficit-cutting target that forms part of IMF terms for a current standby loan.
